At the edge of town, where the last streetlamp gives up and the road turns to gravel, there’s a little field that looks ordinary by day.

At night, it gathers the stars.

Not all of them—just the ones people have misplaced. A wish whispered into a pillow. A name forgotten at the tip of the tongue. The small, bright certainty you had as a child that the world was waiting to be kind.

They settle in the grass like dew.

In the morning, nobody sees them. But people walk home from the field a little lighter, carrying something they can’t quite name. A tune they haven’t heard in years. The courage to make a phone call. A sudden urge to open the curtains.

And the stars, having done their quiet work, rise again.
